title: The Three Modes Side by Side, and What DMA Does to a Cache
quickIdea: Programmed I/O wastes the CPU in the wait, interrupt-driven I/O removes the wait but pays per word, DMA removes the per-word CPU work and pays a small setup. The price of DMA is a second bus master and a cache that can go stale.
remember: Bulk throughput: DMA highest, then interrupt-driven, then programmed I/O - the ordering of GATE CSE 2022 Q.17.
CPU utilisation, best first: DMA, interrupt-driven, programmed I/O. Programmed I/O is worst, not best, which is the false statement of 2024 Set 1 Q.15.
Programmed I/O remains the simplest and is adequate for a rarely-ready slow device when the wait is short.
DMA needs a bus arbiter, a second master, a completion interrupt, and cache maintenance.

Cache coherence: if the controller writes memory while a cached copy exists, the cached copy is stale; if a dirty cached block is not written back before the controller reads memory, the controller reads stale data. Either flush the block, or use a non-cacheable buffer.

example.prompt: A 500-byte block must move from a device to memory. Compare the three schemes on the figures already established: programmed I/O polling the device per byte, the interrupt routine at 7 cycles per byte plus 2, and DMA at 20 cycles plus 2 per byte.
example.work: Interrupt-driven: 2 + 500 x 7 = 3502 cycles. DMA: 20 + 500 x 2 = 1020 cycles. Programmed I/O pays the same per-byte loop as the interrupt routine plus the polling wait, so it is worse than 3502 cycles in CPU time.
example.answer: DMA at 1020 cycles, interrupt-driven at 3502, programmed I/O above that - the ordering the exam tests.

gateAngle: The comparison is asked as a single statement question more often than any other form in this topic: 2022 Q.17 (highest throughput), 2024 Set 1 Q.15 (which comparison is false). The cache-coherence caveat is not yet a verified GATE CSE question here, so it is taught as the reason DMA is not free.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2022 Q.17: which facilitates bulk transfer from hard disk to memory with the highest throughput?
variations.why: Interrupt-driven and programmed I/O both put the CPU in the data path, so the rate is capped by the service routine rather than by the bus.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A device produces one byte every 10 ms. Which scheme is appropriate, and why not DMA?
variations.answer: Interrupt-driven I/O, or even polling if the CPU has nothing else to do. DMA is inappropriate because its setup and completion overhead would exceed the cost of the single byte.
variations.why: DMA's fixed cost is only worth paying when many units move per setup.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A DMA controller writes a block into a region that is currently cached with write-back policy. What can go wrong, and what are the two fixes?
variations.answer: The cached copy becomes stale, so a later read returns the old data. Fixes: flush or invalidate the affected cache blocks around the transfer, or map the buffer as non-cacheable.
variations.why: It is the standard DMA/cache interaction, and it is why device drivers call cache-maintenance routines.

trap.what: Treating DMA as strictly better than the other two modes in every case, or forgetting that a DMA write can invalidate a cache line.
trap.why: DMA's setup, arbitration and completion interrupt are fixed costs that a single-byte transfer cannot amortise; and a second bus master writing memory behind the cache's back breaks the assumption that memory and cache agree.
trap.counterexample: One byte from a slow sensor: DMA pays 20 cycles of setup for 2 cycles of transfer, while a single interrupt costs about 7. The fixed cost dominates, so DMA is the wrong tool.

check.question: Rank the three schemes by CPU utilisation, best first, and state the single reason for the ranking.
check.answer: DMA, then interrupt-driven, then programmed I/O - the ranking follows how much per-word work the CPU still does, from none to all of it plus the waiting.
check.explanation: Utilisation is about what the CPU is free to do; DMA leaves it free for everything except setup and completion.
